content.chapter: Chapter 1: A Roadmap for a Greener Europe
objectives: Explain the Green Deal as a growth strategy and a roadmap.
Explain the 2050 aim.
Explain the shift to a circular economy.
Use participle clauses, serve as and in order to.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter is dense: two long sentences carry the whole definition. Learners unpack the sentences into a definition map (who · when · what · aim · method) before they analyse the formal grammar that makes the text compact.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The European Commission is an EU institution, not a country.
Net zero does not mean no emissions; emissions are balanced by what is removed.
“Announced by …” is not the main verb; the main verb is “serves”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past participle clauses · serve as · by + -ing · in order to
Notice (Activity 1): Announced by the European Commission …, the Green Deal serves as …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *serves like a strategy · *by create · *in order for tackle.
Use (Activity 4): a roadmap for our school.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: sus-TAIN-a-ble, ROAD-map, in-I-ti-a-tive, ef-FI-cient-ly, trans-for-MA-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the difference between a plan and a roadmap?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the Green Deal?
Second reading: unpack the first sentence into a definition map.
Find how the circular economy protects nature.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Definition map; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a roadmap for our school; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the text call the Green Deal both a growth strategy and a roadmap?
How does the shift to a circular economy protect nature?
Why does the writer use such long sentences in this chapter?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Growth Strategy” and “Using Resources Efficiently” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: sustainable, greenhouse gas, emissions, circular economy.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the definition map with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite the first sentence as three short sentences, then compare the effect.

formativeAssessment: Explains what the Green Deal is.
Uses participle clauses or in order to correctly.
expectedResponses: Announced in 2019, the Green Deal serves as the EU’s growth strategy for sustainable development. It aims to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions to zero by 2050 by creating a clean economy and promoting the shift to a circular economy.
content.transferTask: Present a green roadmap for your school.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners unpack the long sentences before analysing them?

exitTicket: Write one sentence that starts with a past participle clause.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains what the Green Deal is.
Uses participle clauses or in order to.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners summarize the purpose of the Green Deal in two sentences, using “roadmap” and “circular economy”. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A summarizes paragraph 1 and B summarizes paragraph 2. Each partner asks a follow-up question about the other’s summary.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the first sentence. Asker asks “What is the subject of the main clause?” Explainer explains the opening participle phrase.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: An exchange student asks why the EU calls the Green Deal a “roadmap”. The learner explains the metaphor and the plan.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The Green Deal is the EU’s roadmap for making its economy, industry, and everyday life more environmentally friendly in order to tackle the climate crisis and ensure a healthier planet.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the European Green Deal is and why it is called a roadmap. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why might the writer call it a ‘growth strategy’ rather than only an environmental plan?” (It aims to grow the economy while protecting the planet.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain “roadmap” as a metaphor and give the 2050 goal.

thinkAloud.sentence: Announced by the European Commission on 11 December 2019, the Green Deal serves as a growth strategy for sustainable development, which aims to protect the planet by creating a clean economy and reducing the EU’s net greenhouse gas emissions to zero by 2050.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Announced by” tells me who and when, before the subject appears. The core is “the Green Deal serves as a growth strategy”. The “which” clause gives its aims. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “A major goal of this initiative is to use resources more efficiently by promoting the shift to a circular economy, focusing on recycling materials and reducing waste to protect nature.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What does the circular economy focus on?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: What would a “roadmap” for a greener school include?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one more step.

objectives: Explain the three key priorities.
Explain the 2030 and 2050 targets.
Explain what sustainability includes.
Use preposition + -ing and formal nouns.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is a structured list under three headings. Learners build a priority table (heading · aim · target or examples) and notice how formal policy writing uses nouns (depletion, loss, commitment) instead of verbs.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The 55% target is for 2030; climate neutrality is for 2050.
“To” in “commitment to” is a preposition, so it takes -ing, not the base verb.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: preposition + -ing (step toward limiting, commitment to protecting) · nominalization (depletion, loss, commitment) · as follows
Notice (Activity 1): This is a critical step toward limiting the effects …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then turn verbs into nouns.
Likely errors: *a commitment to protect · *step toward limit.
Use (Activity 4): our city’s priorities.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: pri-OR-i-ties, de-PLE-tion, bi-o-di-VER-si-ty, com-MIT-ment, neu-TRAL-i-ty.
beforeReading: Ask: “What is the difference between a priority and a wish?”
duringReading: First reading: What are the three key priorities?
Second reading: complete the priority table.
Find the 2030 and 2050 targets.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Priority table; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: our city’s priorities; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the text call climate neutrality a critical step?
What does the sustainable use of natural resources mean?
How can economic growth be sustainable?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Critical Step” and “Healthy Soil” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: climate neutrality, deforestation, depletion, biodiversity.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the table with the three headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that compares the 2030 and 2050 targets.

formativeAssessment: Uses preposition + -ing or formal nouns correctly.
expectedResponses: The EU aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 and achieve climate neutrality by 2050. The Green Deal also aims to prevent deforestation, the depletion of water resources and the loss of biodiversity.
content.transferTask: Write on the key environmental priorities of your city.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the formal nouns in the text?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “a step toward …-ing”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners present the three key priorities and explain how they depend on each other. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A explains the first two priorities and B explains the third. Together they write one sentence that links all three.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads “Sustainability”. Asker asks “Which three environmental problems does it name?” Explainer explains “depletion”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A local mayor asks which priority should come first in a small town. The learner argues for one with reasons.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “In this way, it seeks to support economic growth in a sustainable manner.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, the three key priorities of the Green Deal. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “How can economic growth and environmental protection support each other?” (Green technologies create jobs while reducing harm.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the 2030 and 2050 targets and explain “climate neutrality” and “biodiversity”.

thinkAloud.sentence: Within this framework, the EU and its member states aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Within this framework” links this target to the priority before it. The sentence has two aims joined by “and”, with two different deadlines. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “The key priorities of the Green Deal are as follows:”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What does the Green Deal aim to ensure for all?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences: Which priority affects your daily life most?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with a different view.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: Why Is the Green Deal Essential?
objectives: Explain why the Green Deal is essential.
Explain what energy security means and why it is a challenge.
Explain how conflicts affect supply chains.
Use formal linkers and the present perfect in an argument.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is a two-step argument: (1) old models are unsustainable, so a net-zero economy is needed; (2) energy is insecure, which makes the change urgent. An argument map (claim → reason → evidence → conclusion) helps learners see the logic.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Energy security means having safe, reliable energy at a fair price, not only having enough energy.
“Indeed” adds support; it is not a contrast linker.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: therefore · indeed · as a result · present perfect (has become, have seriously weakened) · pose a risk
Notice (Activity 1): Therefore, … Indeed, …
Build (Activities 2–3): fill the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Therefore of this · *Indeed, but … · *has became.
Use (Activity 4): a short argument.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: deg-ra-DA-tion, ge-o-po-LIT-i-cal, com-pet-I-tive-ness, dis-RUP-tions, SCARCE.
duringReading: First reading: Why is the Green Deal essential?
Second reading: complete the argument map.
Find why supply chains may face disruptions.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Argument map; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a short argument; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why are traditional economic models no longer sustainable?
What creates constant uncertainty around the world?
How do broken supply chains weaken companies?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “No Longer Sustainable” and “Energy Security” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: fossil fuels, net-zero, transitioning, geopolitical.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the argument map with the claim written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a summary of the argument in three sentences with three different linkers.

formativeAssessment: Explains why the Green Deal is essential.
expectedResponses: Traditional economic models are no longer sustainable. Therefore, a net-zero economy is seen as the key way to tackle the climate crisis. Indeed, energy security has become a critical challenge, because conflicts threaten trade routes.
content.transferTask: Write an argument about energy security.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the argument from claim to conclusion?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Therefore” and one with “Indeed”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why the Green Deal is essential.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why the Green Deal is essential, linking the environmental and the energy argument. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner explains paragraph 1 to a partner. The partner explains paragraph 2 and says how it supports paragraph 1.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about supply chains. Asker asks “Why may supply chains face disruptions?” Explainer explains the causes.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A business owner complains about energy costs. The learner explains the wider causes and one solution from the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Traditional economic models that rely on heavy resource consumption and fossil fuels are no longer sustainable.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why the Green Deal is essential for the environment and for energy security. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “How does the writer move from the environment to energy security?” (Both show that the old model cannot continue.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain “energy security” and use “Therefore” or “As a result” to link causes and effects.

thinkAloud.sentence: Therefore, transitioning to a net-zero economy is seen as the key way to tackle the climate crisis, protect biodiversity, and ensure long-term energy security.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Therefore” draws a conclusion from the sentence before: old models are not sustainable. The conclusion has three aims. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “The Green Deal is crucial because climate change and environmental degradation pose a severe risk to the planet.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Why have many companies lost competitiveness?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences about how a global crisis affected energy prices where you live.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Switch to Renewable Energy
objectives: Explain why countries are switching to renewable energy.
Explain what industrial success requires.
Explain what a comprehensive strategy should be based on.
Use gerund subjects and verb patterns.
content.pedagogy: The chapter offers the solution to the problem in Chapter 3. A problem–solution–requirements chart links the two chapters and organizes the three requirements.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Renewable energy is “often” cheaper, not always.
A gerund subject takes a singular verb: Sustaining … will require / Sustaining … requires.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: gerund subjects · require + -ing · call for + noun · provide someone with something
Notice (Activity 1): Sustaining industrial success … will require …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Sustain industrial success will … · *calls a faster transition · *provide industries affordable energy.
Use (Activity 4): a strategy proposal.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: com-pre-HEN-sive, af-FORD-a-ble, de-PEN-den-cy, in-VEST-ment, in-no-VA-tion.
duringReading: First reading: What are countries switching to?
Second reading: complete the chart.
Find what the strategy should be based on.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a strategy proposal; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why are countries switching to renewable energy?
What three things does industrial success require?
Why should a strategy be based on a detailed analysis?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Wind and Solar Power” and “A Comprehensive Strategy” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: renewable energy.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the problem from Chapter 3 written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that links the problem in Chapter 3 with the solution in Chapter 4.

formativeAssessment: Explains why countries switch to renewable energy.
Uses gerund subjects or verb patterns correctly.
expectedResponses: A growing number of countries are switching to renewable energy, which is often cheaper. Sustaining industrial success will require changing policies, moving toward renewable energy, and training workers with new skills.
content.transferTask: Write a renewable energy strategy proposal for your town.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link this chapter with the problem in Chapter 3?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with a gerund subject.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the end of the first paragraph.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses gerund subjects or verb patterns.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why and how countries switch to renewable energy. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A explains paragraph 1 and B explains paragraph 2. Each partner identifies one condition for success.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the first sentence. Asker asks “What three purposes does it give?” Explainer lists the infinitives.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A town council debates building a wind farm. The learner argues for it using the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “This situation calls for a faster green transition to provide industries with affordable clean energy.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why countries are switching to renewable energy and what they need for success. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What should the comprehensive strategy be based on?” (A detailed analysis of investment needs.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give three purposes of the switch and three requirements.

thinkAloud.sentence: To prevent these financial burdens, replace expensive fossil fuels, and end dependency on these traditional fuels, a growing number of countries are taking important steps to switch to renewable energy, such as wind and solar power, which is often cheaper.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The sentence starts with three “to” purposes. The main clause comes after the comma: countries are taking steps. I read the purposes as the reasons. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Sustaining industrial success in these uncertain times will require changing policies, moving toward renewable energy, and training workers with new skills.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What should governments design?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences about one renewable energy project you would support in your region.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Birth of a Net-Zero Era
objectives: Explain the net-zero era.
Explain which countries can become global leaders.
Name the technologies in the Net-Zero Industry Act.
Use likely to, consequently and both … and.
content.pedagogy: The chapter forecasts the future. Learners notice how the writer hedges (are likely to, can) and build a future map (markets · technology · industries · law). The technical words are supported by pictures.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Net-Zero Industry Act is an EU law, not a company.
“Are likely to” is a prediction, not a certainty.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be likely to (hedged prediction) · consequently · both … and · bring with it · lead to the creation of
Notice (Activity 1): The coming decades are likely to see …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *are likely seeing · *both in technology or in … · *Consequently of this.
Use (Activity 4): a forecast.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: DEC-ades, e-MERG-ing, mod-ern-IZ-ing, TUR-bines, car-bon di-OX-ide.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which jobs will be common in 2050?”
duringReading: First reading: What will the net-zero era bring?
Second reading: complete the future map.
Find the technologies in the law.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Future map; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a forecast; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does the net-zero era bring with it?
Why can early investors secure a strong place?
What does the Net-Zero Industry Act help build?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Net-Zero Era” and “The Net-Zero Industry Act” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: eco-friendly.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give picture cards of the five technologies.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short news report about the Net-Zero Industry Act with one hedged prediction.

formativeAssessment: Names the technologies in the law.
Uses likely to or consequently correctly.
expectedResponses: The coming decades are likely to see the birth of a net-zero era. Consequently, countries that invest first can secure a strong place in the new economy. The Net-Zero Industry Act helps build batteries, wind turbines, heat pumps and solar panels.
content.transferTask: Write a forecast about your country’s economy.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners notice the hedging in the chapter?

exitTicket: Write one prediction with “is likely to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the technologies in the law.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain the economic opportunities of the net-zero era. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A explains paragraph 1 and B explains paragraph 2. Each partner asks one follow-up question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the definition of the net-zero era. Asker asks “What is balanced?” Explainer explains “balanced by”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A careers adviser tells a student which skills will matter in the net-zero era. The learner speaks as the adviser.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Consequently, countries that choose to invest first and move faster today can secure a strong place in this emerging economy.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the net-zero era is and which opportunities it brings. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer say ‘are likely to see’ rather than ‘will see’?” (It is a careful prediction.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners define net-zero precisely and name four technologies in the Act.

thinkAloud.sentence: The coming decades are likely to see the birth of a net-zero era, a period when the greenhouse gases we release are balanced by the amount we remove from the air.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The phrase after the comma renames “a net-zero era” and defines it. “Balanced by” means the two amounts are equal. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “This new economic structure brings with it fresh markets, advanced clean technologies, and a complete transformation of our existing energy systems.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What does the Net-Zero Industry Act help to build?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences about a skill you would like to learn for a green job.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: New Rules for Greener Products
objectives: Explain the ban on destroying unsold clothing.
Explain the requirement for spare parts.
Explain what the rules mean for factories and governments.
Use formal noun phrases.
content.pedagogy: The chapter presents regulations in formal noun phrases. Learners unpack each rule (noun phrase → plain verb phrase) and then draft their own regulation in the same formal style.
anticipatedMisconceptions: A ban on + -ing, not *a ban to.
“Apply to” here means “be relevant to”, not “ask for a job”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: a ban on + -ing · a requirement to + verb · apply to · give priority to + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): … strict bans on destroying unsold clothing, as well as requirements to make spare parts …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *ban to destroy · *requirement of make · *apply for products.
Use (Activity 4): draft a regulation.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: reg-u-LA-tions, re-QUIRE-ments, ac-CES-si-ble, sus-tain-a-BIL-i-ty, pri-OR-i-ty.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why would a shop destroy clothes that it could not sell?”
duringReading: First reading: What examples of rules does the chapter give?
Second reading: unpack each rule into plain language.
Find what governments will give top priority to.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Unpacking the rules; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: draft a regulation; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is destroying unsold clothing a problem for the environment?
How do accessible spare parts support a circular economy?
What will the regulations apply to in the future?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Strict Bans” and “Accessible Spare Parts” when the picture is in place.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: There is a ban on … / There is a requirement to …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite the whole chapter in plain language for younger learners.

formativeAssessment: Explains what factories will need to do.
expectedResponses: The new rules include strict bans on destroying unsold clothing and requirements to make spare parts easily accessible for repairs. In the future, these regulations will apply to a much broader range of everyday products.
content.transferTask: Draft a regulation for products sold at your school.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners move confidently between formal and plain language?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “a ban on …-ing”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains what factories will need to do.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the end of the chapter.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how product rules support a sustainable economy. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner explains the two examples to a partner. The partner explains how each one reduces waste.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence with “Specific examples”. Asker asks “What are the two examples?” Explainer explains “easily accessible”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A clothing company manager asks why destroying unsold clothes is banned. The learner explains the reasoning.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “In the future, modern regulations will apply to a much broader range of everyday products.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what new rules for green products require. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What will governments give top priority to?” (Developing net-zero technologies.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give two rules and explain who must follow them.

thinkAloud.sentence: Specific examples of these rules include strict bans on destroying unsold clothing, as well as requirements to make spare parts easily accessible for repairs.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Specific examples … include” introduces examples. “As well as” adds the second one. I can list them in my notes. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “These rules help create strong and successful systems for building, reusing, and recycling green technologies around the world.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What will factories need to follow?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences about a product that should be easier to repair.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Everyday Choices and the Future of Work
objectives: Explain why transparent information matters.
Explain what energy labels do.
Explain how the labor market is changing.
Use depend on + noun + -ing and the present perfect continuous.
content.pedagogy: The chapter has two sides: consumers and the labor market. A two-part organizer (Consumers / Workers) helps learners compare them. Real energy labels make the first paragraph concrete.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Energy labels show energy use; they do not show the price.
“Has been increasing” stresses that the rise is continuing now.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: depend on + noun + -ing · allow + person + to · present perfect continuous · instead of
Notice (Activity 1): … depends heavily on consumers making smart, eco-friendly choices …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *depends on consumers make · *allow users compare · *has been increase.
Use (Activity 4): a consumer guide.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: trans-PAR-ent, ap-PLI-an-ces, ef-FORT-less-ly, per-son-NEL, SPE-cial-ized.
beforeReading: Ask: “What information do you want before you buy a product?”
duringReading: First reading: What do consumers need?
Second reading: complete the two-part organizer.
Find how the labor market is changing.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Two-part organizer; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a consumer guide; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the success of the Green Deal depend on consumers?
What should people see before they buy a product?
Why will there be strong competition for specialized talent?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Transparent Information” and “The Labor Market” when the picture is in place.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a picture of an energy label.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short report on the labor market with one present perfect continuous sentence.

formativeAssessment: Explains how the labor market is changing.
expectedResponses: The success of the Green Deal depends heavily on consumers making smart choices driven by transparent information. The number of green jobs has been increasing rapidly, so large-scale training programs are required.
content.transferTask: Write a guide for eco-friendly consumers.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see both sides: consumers and workers?

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain the role of consumers and workers in the green transition. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A explains paragraph 1 and B explains paragraph 2. Each partner gives an example from daily life.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about energy labels. Asker asks “What do they allow users to do?” Explainer explains “effortlessly”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A relative wants to buy the cheapest appliance. The learner explains how energy labels can save money and energy.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Providing consumers with more information is a major step toward a successful green transition.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how consumers and workers are part of the green transition. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What does ‘competition for specialized talent’ mean?” (Companies will compete to hire skilled workers.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain “transparent information” and one effect on the labor market.

thinkAloud.sentence: In fact, the success of the Green Deal depends heavily on consumers making smart, eco-friendly choices driven by transparent information.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Depends heavily on” shows a strong condition. “Driven by” tells me what makes good choices possible: transparent information. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “People should easily see how sustainable, durable, and clean a product is before they buy it.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What is reshaping the labor market?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences about a label or piece of information that helps you shop more responsibly.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: Education and Our Shared Future
objectives: Explain why education is a major part of the Green Deal.
Explain the three areas that depend on education.
Explain why nations should keep working together.
Use concluding language and balanced arguments.
content.pedagogy: The closing chapter concludes the argument: success depends on education and cooperation. Türkiye’s own plan links the text to learners’ country. The policy panel brings the whole book together and asks learners to evaluate, not only summarize.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Türkiye’s plan was published in 2021; its net-zero goal is 2053.
“In conclusion” closes a text; it does not introduce new information.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in conclusion · because of this · depend largely on how well · it is helpful for … to · set a goal of + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): In conclusion, the success … will depend largely on how well …
Build (Activities 2–3): fill the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *In conclusion of · *set a goal to reaching · *depend largely of.
Use (Activity 4): a balanced conclusion.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: TÜR-ki-ye.
Numbers: twenty twenty-one; twenty fifty-three.
Stress: in-ter-con-NECT-ed, pro-duc-TIV-i-ty, in-JUS-tice, FOS-ter-ing.
beforeReading: Ask: “Can education solve the climate crisis?”
duringReading: First reading: What will the success depend on?
Second reading: find the three areas where education matters.
Find Türkiye’s plan and goal.
afterReading: Group task: “The Green Deal: A Policy Panel”.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–17 Three areas; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: a balanced conclusion; 43–45 Exit ticket. (Panel in a second lesson.)
discussionPoints: Why will success depend largely on education?
What does a fair transition that prevents social injustice mean?
Why is it helpful for nations to work with international partners?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “An Informed Society” and “Türkiye’s Plan” when the picture is in place.
The policy panel closes the book; each analyst covers two chapters.
This chapter has no Word Notes.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: In conclusion, … However, …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a balanced conclusion for the whole book in five sentences.

formativeAssessment: Explains why nations should work together.
expectedResponses: In conclusion, the success of the green transition will depend largely on education and workforce training. In an interconnected world, nations should keep working with their international partners. Türkiye set a goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2053.
content.transferTask: Write a balanced conclusion about education and the climate crisis.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners evaluate the role of education, not only describe it?

exitTicket: Write one sentence that starts with “In conclusion”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why education and international cooperation are essential for the Green Deal. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A explains paragraph 1 and B explains paragraph 2. Each partner asks a follow-up question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about three areas. Asker asks “Which three areas does education support?” Explainer explains “fair transition”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: At a school assembly, the learner gives a one-minute talk on why green skills matter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Fostering an informed and aware society through education and workforce training is essential for the world’s shared future.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why education matters for the Green Deal and what Türkiye’s plan aims for. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What does ‘a fair transition that prevents social injustice’ mean?” (The change should not harm some groups more than others.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give three areas that education supports and Türkiye’s target year.

thinkAloud.sentence: Fostering an informed and aware society through education and workforce training is essential for the world’s shared future.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The subject is a long “-ing” phrase. I find the verb “is” and see the main claim: this is essential. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “In conclusion, the success of the green transition will depend largely on how well nations can train workers and educate society.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: When did Türkiye publish its Green Deal Action Plan?

onlineTask.post: Post three sentences about one green skill every student should learn.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

metadata.title: The European Green Deal B2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Our World Today
metadata.estimatedDuration: 8 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow extended informational texts about society, economy and the environment, and who can produce clear, detailed explanations, evaluations and arguments.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through an extended informational text about the European Green Deal: its roadmap and priorities, energy security, the switch to renewable energy, the net-zero era, new regulations, consumers and the labor market, education and Türkiye’s own plan, using the Language Focus attached to every chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. At B2, learners also notice how the writer signals certainty (are likely to / may / can) and builds a formal argument (therefore / indeed / consequently / in conclusion), and they use these forms in their own writing.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 8 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a picture of a label or a machine, or a link to the previous chapter.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a definition map, a priority table, an argument map, a problem–solution chart, a future map, formal rules unpacked into plain language or a two-part organizer.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B2 transfer: an explanation, proposal or argument about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets, Key Terms and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the chapter sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? How certain is the writer?), let learners formulate the rule, then confirm it and practice it in context. B2 targets include participle clauses, preposition + -ing, nominalization, gerund subjects, hedged predictions, formal noun patterns, the present perfect continuous and formal linkers. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: past participle clauses · serve as · by + -ing · in order to
Ch2: preposition + -ing (step toward limiting, commitment to protecting) · nominalization (depletion, loss, commitment) · as follows
Ch3: therefore · indeed · as a result · present perfect (has become, have seriously weakened) · pose a risk
Ch4: gerund subjects · require + -ing · call for + noun · provide someone with something
Ch5: be likely to (hedged prediction) · consequently · both … and · bring with it · lead to the creation of
Ch6: a ban on + -ing · a requirement to + verb · apply to · give priority to + -ing
Ch7: depend on + noun + -ing · allow + person + to · present perfect continuous · instead of
Ch8: in conclusion · because of this · depend largely on how well · it is helpful for … to · set a goal of + -ing

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow extended narration for gist, arguments and key details.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify arguments, degrees of certainty, causes, results and policy details.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: explain and evaluate ideas, propose policies and present balanced positions.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce clear, detailed B2 paragraphs and short arguments with evidence, hedging and balanced conclusions.

valuesFocus: D16 Responsibility — Caring for nature and the shared future.
D5 Sensitivity — Noticing what nature and people need.
D20 Helpfulness — Working together across borders.
D1 Justice — A fair transition for all.
languageFocus: Every one of the 8 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, long sentences unpacked, charts given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for evaluation, counterpoints and evidence from more than one chapter, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside numbers or opinions.
The book is about EU policy; Türkiye’s own plan (2021, net zero by 2053) is in Chapter 8. Present both as the book gives them.
Discuss energy and money at home with care; some families may have difficulties paying their bills.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The Green Deal connects with questions every community faces today: how to use less energy, how to protect nature and how to work together across borders.

themes.title: An interconnected world:
themes.description: The green transition extends across all borders (Chapter 8). Discuss why nations need international partners.

themes.title: Energy security:
themes.description: Regional conflicts can block trade routes and make energy scarce (Chapter 3). Discuss how this affects families in different countries.

themes.title: Repair, not replace:
themes.description: New rules make spare parts easily accessible for repairs (Chapter 6). Discuss repair traditions in your culture.

themes.title: A fair transition:
themes.description: Education is important for a fair transition that prevents social injustice (Chapter 8). Discuss who might be left behind and how to help them.

actions: Find the energy label on a machine at home and read it.
Repair or reuse one old thing this week.
Find Türkiye’s Green Deal Action Plan goal year on a class poster.

exitTicket: One idea from today’s chapter, with the sentence that supports it, is …
One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week for a greener world is …

miniProject.title: The Green Deal: A Policy Panel
miniProject.desc: In groups, each member becomes an analyst for two chapters: strategy, energy, industry or society. Prepare a two-minute statement with one quotation, hold a panel discussion and agree on three recommendations.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Policy Brief
reflectivePrompt.desc: The success of the green transition will depend largely on education (Chapter 8). Write eight to ten sentences arguing which part of the Green Deal matters most for your country. Use evidence from the book and one counterpoint.

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D16 Responsibility
items.value: Responsibility: The Green Deal stresses the sustainable use of natural resources and a commitment to protecting and restoring the environment (Chapter 2).

items.label: D5 Sensitivity
items.value: Sensitivity: Clear and accessible data helps individuals choose green products instead of high-emission options (Chapter 7).

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness: It is helpful for nations to keep working closely with their international partners (Chapter 8).

items.label: D1 Justice
items.value: Justice: Education is important for a fair transition that prevents social injustice (Chapter 8).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR B2. The table links the B2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test B2 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can read with a large degree of independence, adapting style and speed of reading to different texts and purposes, and using appropriate reference sources selectively.
practice: Chapter 3 (Why Is the Green Deal Essential?): Follow the argument from claim to conclusion.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write clear, detailed texts on a variety of subjects related to his field of interest, synthesising and evaluating information and arguments from a number of sources.
practice: Chapter 3 (Why Is the Green Deal Essential?): Write an argument about energy security.
Chapter 8 (Education and Our Shared Future): Write a balanced conclusion.
Language Review, “Use: A Policy Brief”: Write an argument with evidence and a counterpoint.

rows.descriptor: Can give clear, systematically developed descriptions and presentations, with appropriate highlighting of significant points, and relevant supporting detail.
practice: Chapter 4 (The Switch to Renewable Energy): Present a strategy proposal for your town.
Chapter 8 (Education and Our Shared Future): Present your analyst statement in the policy panel.

test.title: End-of-Level Test B2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 85 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (50 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (35 minutes): on paper. Write an essay discussing this statement: “Travel teaches us more than books do.” (180–220 words)
Speaking (about 10 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 3 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

content.chapter: Chapter 1: A Roadmap for a Greener Europe
objectives: I can explain the Green Deal as a growth strategy and a roadmap.
I can explain how the shift to a circular economy protects nature.
I can use participle clauses and in order to in formal writing.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “Announced by the European Commission …, the Green Deal serves as …”: a participle clause. Then choose the forms and rewrite three sentences.
content.lessonPlan: What is a roadmap? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find what the Green Deal is. Make a definition map.
discussionPoints: The Green Deal aims to use resources more efficiently. Which resource could you use more efficiently at home?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Growth Strategy” and “Using Resources Efficiently” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the end of the first paragraph again. Find “in order to”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a formal paragraph of six to seven sentences presenting a green roadmap for your school.

whatToNotice: The Green Deal is both a growth strategy and a roadmap.
A circular economy focuses on recycling and reducing waste.
readListen: What is a roadmap? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find what the Green Deal is.
Make a definition map.
findAnswerInStory: Find when the Green Deal was announced.
Find the 2050 aim.
Find what the master plan offers.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: sustainable, greenhouse gas, emissions, circular economy.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose why the EU wants to change its economy. Read the end of the first paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the end of the first paragraph again.
selfCheck: Can I explain what the Green Deal is?
Can I explain the circular economy?
Can I use participle clauses?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a formal paragraph of six to seven sentences presenting a green roadmap for your school.
content.reflectionPrompt: The Green Deal aims to use resources more efficiently. Which resource could you use more efficiently at home?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Summarize the purpose of the Green Deal in two sentences, using “roadmap” and “circular economy”. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “The Green Deal is the EU’s roadmap for making its economy, industry, and everyday life more environmentally friendly in order to tackle the climate crisis and ensure a healthier planet.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, what the European Green Deal is and why it is called a roadmap.

thinkAloud.sentence: Announced by the European Commission on 11 December 2019, the Green Deal serves as a growth strategy for sustainable development, which aims to protect the planet by creating a clean economy and reducing the EU’s net greenhouse gas emissions to zero by 2050.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Announced by” tells me who and when, before the subject appears. The core is “the Green Deal serves as a growth strategy”. The “which” clause gives its aims. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “A major goal of this initiative is to use resources more efficiently by promoting the shift to a circular economy, focusing on recycling materials and reducing waste to protect nature.”
stopAndCheck.question: What does the circular economy focus on? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can explain the three key priorities of the Green Deal.
I can explain the 2030 and 2050 targets and why they matter.
I can use step toward + -ing and formal nouns such as depletion and commitment.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “a critical step toward limiting the effects”: preposition + -ing. Then choose the forms and turn three verbs into nouns.
content.lessonPlan: What is a priority? Write one priority for your town. Read the chapter and find the three key priorities. Make a priority table.
discussionPoints: The Green Deal stresses the sustainable use of natural resources. How could your family use water more sustainably?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Critical Step” and “Healthy Soil” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the Sustainability paragraph again. Find “such as”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a formal paragraph of six to seven sentences on the three key environmental priorities of your city.

whatToNotice: Formal texts use nouns like depletion and loss.
readListen: What is a priority? Write one priority for your town.
Read the chapter and find the three key priorities.
Make a priority table.
findAnswerInStory: Find the 2030 target.
Find the 2050 target.
Find what the Green Deal aims to ensure for all.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: climate neutrality, deforestation, depletion, biodiversity.
“The depletion of water resources.” What does depletion mean?
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose which problems the Green Deal aims to prevent. Read the Sustainability paragraph.
selfCheck: Can I explain the three priorities?
Can I explain the two targets?
Can I use preposition + -ing?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a formal paragraph of six to seven sentences on the three key environmental priorities of your city.
content.reflectionPrompt: The Green Deal stresses the sustainable use of natural resources. How could your family use water more sustainably?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Present the three key priorities and explain how they depend on each other. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “In this way, it seeks to support economic growth in a sustainable manner.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, the three key priorities of the Green Deal.

thinkAloud.sentence: Within this framework, the EU and its member states aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Within this framework” links this target to the priority before it. The sentence has two aims joined by “and”, with two different deadlines. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “The key priorities of the Green Deal are as follows:”
stopAndCheck.question: What does the Green Deal aim to ensure for all? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: Why Is the Green Deal Essential?
objectives: I can explain why the Green Deal is essential.
I can explain why energy security has become a critical challenge.
I can use formal linkers and the present perfect to build an argument.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “Therefore, …” and “Indeed, …”: a conclusion and extra support. Then fill the linkers and rewrite three sentences.
content.lessonPlan: What does energy security mean? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find why the Green Deal is essential. Make an argument map.
discussionPoints: Energy-intensive industries suffer most from high prices. Which energy-intensive habit could you change?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “No Longer Sustainable” and “Energy Security” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the end of the second paragraph again. Find “because ongoing conflicts”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write an argument of six to seven sentences about energy security.

whatToNotice: Traditional economic models are no longer sustainable.
Energy security has become a critical challenge.
readListen: What does energy security mean? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find why the Green Deal is essential.
Make an argument map.
findAnswerInStory: Find what traditional models rely on.
Find what is seen as the key way.
Find what conflicts threaten to block.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: fossil fuels, net-zero, transitioning, geopolitical.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose why supply chains may face disruptions. Read the end of the second paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the end of the second paragraph again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why the Green Deal is essential?
Can I explain energy security?
Can I use formal linkers?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write an argument of six to seven sentences about energy security.
content.reflectionPrompt: Energy-intensive industries suffer most from high prices. Which energy-intensive habit could you change?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain why the Green Deal is essential, linking the environmental and the energy argument. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Traditional economic models that rely on heavy resource consumption and fossil fuels are no longer sustainable.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, why the Green Deal is essential for the environment and for energy security.

thinkAloud.sentence: Therefore, transitioning to a net-zero economy is seen as the key way to tackle the climate crisis, protect biodiversity, and ensure long-term energy security.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Therefore” draws a conclusion from the sentence before: old models are not sustainable. The conclusion has three aims. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “The Green Deal is crucial because climate change and environmental degradation pose a severe risk to the planet.”
stopAndCheck.question: Why have many companies lost competitiveness? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Switch to Renewable Energy
objectives: I can explain why countries are switching to renewable energy.
I can explain what industrial success requires.
I can use gerund subjects and require / call for + noun.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “Sustaining industrial success … will require …”: an -ing subject. Then choose the forms and rewrite three sentences.
content.lessonPlan: What problem did Chapter 3 describe? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find what countries are switching to. Make a problem–solution chart.
discussionPoints: Countries want to end their dependency on fossil fuels. Which dependency in your daily life would you like to reduce?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Wind and Solar Power” and “A Comprehensive Strategy” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the beginning of the second paragraph again. Find “calls for”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a formal proposal of six to seven sentences for a renewable energy strategy in your town.

readListen: What problem did Chapter 3 describe? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find what countries are switching to.
Make a problem–solution chart.
findAnswerInStory: Find two kinds of renewable energy.
Find what industrial success will require.
Find what the strategy should be based on.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose why a faster transition is needed. Read the beginning of the second paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the beginning of the second paragraph again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why countries switch?
Can I explain what success requires?
Can I use a gerund subject?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a formal proposal of six to seven sentences for a renewable energy strategy in your town.
content.reflectionPrompt: Countries want to end their dependency on fossil fuels. Which dependency in your daily life would you like to reduce?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain why and how countries switch to renewable energy. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “This situation calls for a faster green transition to provide industries with affordable clean energy.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, why countries are switching to renewable energy and what they need for success.

thinkAloud.sentence: To prevent these financial burdens, replace expensive fossil fuels, and end dependency on these traditional fuels, a growing number of countries are taking important steps to switch to renewable energy, such as wind and solar power, which is often cheaper.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: The sentence starts with three “to” purposes. The main clause comes after the comma: countries are taking steps. I read the purposes as the reasons. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “Sustaining industrial success in these uncertain times will require changing policies, moving toward renewable energy, and training workers with new skills.”
stopAndCheck.question: What should governments design? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Birth of a Net-Zero Era
objectives: I can explain what the net-zero era will bring.
I can explain which countries can become global leaders.
I can use likely to, consequently and both … and.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “The coming decades are likely to see …”: a hedged prediction. Then choose the forms and rewrite three sentences.
content.lessonPlan: Which jobs will be common in 2050? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find what the net-zero era will bring. Make a future map.
discussionPoints: New industries require newly skilled workers. Which skill would prepare you for a green job?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “A Net-Zero Era” and “The Net-Zero Industry Act” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the middle of the first paragraph again. Find “Consequently”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a forecast of six to seven sentences about your country’s economy in a net-zero era.

whatToNotice: The writer says the net-zero era is likely, not certain.
The EU introduced a law for green technologies.
readListen: Which jobs will be common in 2050? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find what the net-zero era will bring.
Make a future map.
findAnswerInStory: Find what the new economic structure brings with it.
Find which countries can secure a strong place.
Find the name of the law.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose which countries can lead. Read the middle of the first paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the middle of the first paragraph again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the net-zero era?
Can I name the technologies in the law?
Can I use likely to?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a forecast of six to seven sentences about your country’s economy in a net-zero era.
content.reflectionPrompt: New industries require newly skilled workers. Which skill would prepare you for a green job?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain the economic opportunities of the net-zero era. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Consequently, countries that choose to invest first and move faster today can secure a strong place in this emerging economy.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, what the net-zero era is and which opportunities it brings.

thinkAloud.sentence: The coming decades are likely to see the birth of a net-zero era, a period when the greenhouse gases we release are balanced by the amount we remove from the air.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: The phrase after the comma renames “a net-zero era” and defines it. “Balanced by” means the two amounts are equal. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “This new economic structure brings with it fresh markets, advanced clean technologies, and a complete transformation of our existing energy systems.”
stopAndCheck.question: What does the Net-Zero Industry Act help to build? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: New Rules for Greener Products
objectives: I can explain two specific examples of the new rules.
I can explain what the rules mean for factories and governments.
I can use noun phrases: a ban on …-ing, a requirement to …, apply to.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “strict bans on destroying unsold clothing” and “requirements to make spare parts easily accessible”. Then choose the forms and rewrite three sentences.
content.lessonPlan: Why would a shop destroy unsold clothes? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find the examples of rules. Unpack each rule into plain language.
discussionPoints: Accessible spare parts make repairs easier. What would you repair instead of replacing?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Strict Bans” and “Accessible Spare Parts” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the end of the chapter again. Find “This means”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a short regulation of six to seven sentences for products sold at your school.

whatToNotice: The rules are written as noun phrases.
The rules will apply to more products in the future.
readListen: Why would a shop destroy unsold clothes? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find the examples of rules.
Unpack each rule into plain language.
findAnswerInStory: Find what is banned.
Find what is required.
Find what governments will give top priority to.
vocabularyInContext: This chapter has no Word Notes.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose what factories will need to do. Read the end of the chapter.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the end of the chapter again.
selfCheck: Can I explain the two rules?
Can I explain what factories will need to do?
Can I use ban on and requirement to?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a short regulation of six to seven sentences for products sold at your school.
content.reflectionPrompt: Accessible spare parts make repairs easier. What would you repair instead of replacing?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain how product rules support a sustainable economy. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “In the future, modern regulations will apply to a much broader range of everyday products.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, what new rules for green products require.

thinkAloud.sentence: Specific examples of these rules include strict bans on destroying unsold clothing, as well as requirements to make spare parts easily accessible for repairs.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Specific examples … include” introduces examples. “As well as” adds the second one. I can list them in my notes. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “These rules help create strong and successful systems for building, reusing, and recycling green technologies around the world.”
stopAndCheck.question: What will factories need to follow? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Everyday Choices and the Future of Work
objectives: I can explain why transparent information matters for consumers.
I can explain how the labor market is changing.
I can use depend on + noun + -ing and the present perfect continuous.
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “depends heavily on consumers making smart, eco-friendly choices”. Then choose the forms and rewrite three sentences.
content.lessonPlan: What do you want to know before you buy something? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find what consumers need. Make a two-part organizer.
discussionPoints: Clear and accessible data helps people choose green products. What information will you look for next time you shop?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Transparent Information” and “The Labor Market” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the end of the second paragraph again. Find “As a result”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a guide of six to seven sentences for eco-friendly consumers.

whatToNotice: Green jobs have been increasing rapidly.
readListen: What do you want to know before you buy something? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find what consumers need.
Make a two-part organizer.
findAnswerInStory: Find what people should see before they buy.
Find what energy labels allow.
Find what the shift is creating.
vocabularyInContext: This chapter has no Word Notes.
“Transparent information.” What does transparent mean here?
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose why there will be strong competition for talent. Read the end of the second paragraph.
wrongAnswerSupport: Read the end of the second paragraph again.
selfCheck: Can I explain why information matters?
Can I explain the labor market?
Can I use depend on + -ing?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a guide of six to seven sentences for eco-friendly consumers.
content.reflectionPrompt: Clear and accessible data helps people choose green products. What information will you look for next time you shop?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain the role of consumers and workers in the green transition. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Providing consumers with more information is a major step toward a successful green transition.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, how consumers and workers are part of the green transition.

thinkAloud.sentence: In fact, the success of the Green Deal depends heavily on consumers making smart, eco-friendly choices driven by transparent information.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Depends heavily on” shows a strong condition. “Driven by” tells me what makes good choices possible: transparent information. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “People should easily see how sustainable, durable, and clean a product is before they buy it.”
stopAndCheck.question: What is reshaping the labor market? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: Education and Our Shared Future
objectives: I can explain why education is a major part of the Green Deal.
I can explain why nations should keep working with their partners.
I can use concluding language and a fair transition that prevents …
content.pedagogy: Read and listen for meaning, find the evidence, do the Quick Challenge, then use the chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
content.grammarFocus: Look at “In conclusion, the success … will depend largely on how well nations can train workers”. Then fill the linkers and rewrite three sentences.
content.pronunciationFocus: Say: twenty fifty-three. Stress: in-ter-con-NECT-ed, in-JUS-tice.
content.lessonPlan: Can education solve the climate crisis? Write one idea. Read the chapter and find what the success depends on. Find Türkiye’s plan.
discussionPoints: Leaders, organizations and citizens should all support these steps. Which step can you support as a citizen?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “An Informed Society” and “Türkiye’s Plan” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the second sentence again. Find “a fair transition”. Try again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write a conclusion of six to seven sentences: Can education solve the climate crisis?

whatToNotice: Education is a major part of the Green Deal.
The green transition extends across all borders.
readListen: Can education solve the climate crisis? Write one idea.
Read the chapter and find what the success depends on.
Find Türkiye’s plan.
findAnswerInStory: Find the three areas where education matters.
Find who should support these steps.
Find Türkiye’s goal.
vocabularyInContext: This chapter has no Word Notes.
“An interconnected world.” What does interconnected mean?
Write one sentence with fair transition.
content.quickChallengeGuide: You will choose the kind of transition the chapter mentions. Read the second sentence.
selfCheck: Can I explain why education matters?
Can I explain why nations work together?
Can I write a balanced conclusion?
content.useWhatYouLearned: Language Focus, last activity: Write a conclusion of six to seven sentences: Can education solve the climate crisis?
content.reflectionPrompt: Leaders, organizations and citizens should all support these steps. Which step can you support as a citizen?

noteTaking.focus: Listen again with the book closed. Write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: Use your notes: Explain why education and international cooperation are essential for the Green Deal. Then check one fact in the story.

mediationTasks.translation: Write “Fostering an informed and aware society through education and workforce training is essential for the world’s shared future.” in your home language.
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Tell someone at home, in your home language, why education matters for the Green Deal and what Türkiye’s plan aims for.

thinkAloud.sentence: Fostering an informed and aware society through education and workforce training is essential for the world’s shared future.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: The subject is a long “-ing” phrase. I find the verb “is” and see the main claim: this is essential. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “In conclusion, the success of the green transition will depend largely on how well nations can train workers and educate society.”
stopAndCheck.question: When did Türkiye publish its Green Deal Action Plan? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

metadata.title: The European Green Deal B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the text about the European Green Deal alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 8 chapters of The European Green Deal.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the argument of the Green Deal text from its roadmap to its conclusion.
Evaluate the role of energy, regulation, consumers, education and cooperation with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 8.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One idea from the Green Deal that I think matters most for my country, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 8 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows responsibility, sensitivity, helpfulness and justice. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Responsibility: Responsibility: The Green Deal stresses the sustainable use of natural resources and a commitment to protecting and restoring the environment (Chapter 2).
Sensitivity: Sensitivity: Clear and accessible data helps individuals choose green products instead of high-emission options (Chapter 7).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: It is helpful for nations to keep working closely with their international partners (Chapter 8).
Justice: Justice: Education is important for a fair transition that prevents social injustice (Chapter 8).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 8, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Key Facts
Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Key Terms
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Explain to someone at home in six sentences what the Green Deal is and why it matters, in your home language or in English.
